# Results — Study 50 (High-Water): the 52-week-high effect on the S&P 500, 2000–2026

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Monthly returns of **398 current S&P 500
members** with ≥20y history (Yahoo). Nearness = price ÷ trailing-12-month high; long the top quintile,
short the bottom; momentum (trailing-12-month return) is the control. As-of 2026-06; inputs fingerprint
`c768f59e31fe`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `NONE` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · "A distinct anomaly"? `BUSTED`

George & Hwang's claim has two parts — stocks near their 52-week high out-earn the rest, *and* this is
something different from momentum — and **both fail here**. On tradable large caps the nearness
long-short doesn't earn a premium; it *loses* **−8.4%/yr at a Sharpe of −0.40 (Lo t = −2.2)** — a
significantly *negative* result, the opposite of the claim. And it is **not distinct from momentum**:
the 52-week-high hedge is **0.87 correlated** with the plain 12-month-momentum hedge — the same factor,
relabelled with an anchoring story. (The negative sign owes partly to this large-cap survivor universe,
where mean-reversion in fallen names dominates — cf. [Study 33 Slingshot](../../33-slingshot/) — but
the headline point, that it's momentum in disguise *and* didn't pay, stands.) `BUSTED`.

## Data stamp

- **Universe**: 398 current S&P 500 members, ≥20y history, 2000-01 → 2026-06, 366 months, fingerprint
  `c768f59e31fe` (survivorship-biased, large-cap — stated)

## The nearness long-short didn't pay — and it's just momentum

| | mean/yr | Sharpe | Lo t |
|---|---|---|---|
| 52-week-high nearness | **−8.4%** | **−0.40** | −2.2 |
| 12-month momentum (control) | −0.9% | −0.04 | −0.2 |
| **corr(nearness hedge, momentum hedge)** | | **+0.87** | |

Two findings in one table. First, buying stocks near their high and shorting those far from it *lost*
money over 2000–2026 on large caps. Second — and more important for the *claim* — the nearness signal is
**0.87 correlated** with ordinary momentum: it is not a distinct anomaly, it's momentum measured a
slightly different way.

## It faded, too

| | 52-week-high Sharpe |
|---|---|
| 1999–2012 | −0.52 |
| 2013–on | −0.18 |

Strongly negative early (the dot-com and GFC momentum crashes punished near-high names), drifting toward
zero since — no period delivers the positive premium the strategy promises.

## …and costs only deepen the hole

| cost / trade | net Sharpe |
|---|---|
| gross | −0.40 |
| 5 bp | −0.45 |
| 10 bp | −0.49 |
| 20 bp | −0.58 |

Since the gross hedge is already negative, turnover costs simply make a losing strategy lose more.

## The honest takeaway

The 52-week-high effect is `BUSTED` on two counts: on tradable large caps it produced a *negative*
long-short (significantly so), and it is **0.87 correlated with plain momentum** — not the distinct
anomaly George & Hwang argued for, but momentum with an anchoring narrative. Whatever the original
1963–2001 sample showed, on the modern, tradable large-cap cross-section there is no separate
52-week-high premium to harvest. `NONE`, `MIRAGE`, distinct-anomaly claim `BUSTED`.
